amstar2_items.justification: No PICO framework is used. As a scoping review, the research questions and eligibility criteria specify the population/setting (forcibly displaced persons in the transitional phase, 6 months to 2 years post-displacement) and broad environmental health conditions, exposures, outcomes, obstacles, and recommendations, without defining a specific intervention or comparator.

No registered protocol (e.g., PROSPERO or OSF) or explicit statement that review methods were established in a written protocol prior to conducting the review is reported, nor are protocol deviations discussed; the authors state only that they followed PRISMA/JBI scoping review guidance and shared search/exclusion criteria with two companion reviews (Behnke et al., 2020; Shackelford et al., 2020).

The authors exclude opinion pieces, letters, news articles, and newsletters lacking new data or analysis (Table 3), but provide no methodological justification for pooling primary empirical designs alongside 18 secondary literature reviews, 2 guidelines, and 1 simulation (Table 5) within the same 88-study synthesis.

Four peer-reviewed databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, EBSCOhost Global Health) and nine grey literature repositories were searched, full search strings were provided in Supplements S1 and S2, and the post-1945 date cutoff was justified; however, the English-only restriction (which excluded 125 full-text records) was not methodologically justified (noted only as a limitation), reference lists/experts were not systematically consulted, and searches (Oct 2017/Jan 2018) predated acceptance/publication by over 24 months.
Both title/abstract and full-text screening were conducted independently in duplicate in Covidence by a five-reviewer team, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer (Section 2.1, p. 5).

Data extraction categories are listed in Table 4, and Section 5.5 mentions working to minimize human error during extraction, but there is no statement that data extraction was performed independently in duplicate or verified on a sample for >=80% agreement.

Figure 1 reports aggregate counts of full-text exclusions by reason (n = 818 excluded; plus 219 non-transitional studies from the 307-article parent pool), but no citation list of excluded full-text studies with study-level justifications is provided in the article or referenced in Supplements S1-S4.

Main-text tables report aggregate counts (Tables 5-8, 11) and study-level water/latrine ratios for subsets of studies (Tables 9-10), while Supplements S3 and S4 map study-level environmental conditions, displacement causes, exposures, outcomes, and obstacles; however, full study-level PICO details (sample sizes, study designs per study, comparator details, follow-up timeframes) are not presented in adequate detail in the main report.

Only the four grey literature records were screened for credibility using the AACODS checklist (Section 2.2). No risk-of-bias assessment was performed for the 84 peer-reviewed studies; the authors explicitly state in Section 5.5 that due to the scoping nature of the review they were not able to account for the quality of the data presented.
Although Table 4 sought camp/setting infrastructure funders (reported missing in most papers), the review does not report the funding sources of the individual included research studies.
No meta-analysis or quantitative pooling of effect estimates was conducted; findings were summarized via descriptive study counts/percentages and narrative thematic categories.
Risk of bias of individual included studies was neither assessed nor accounted for when interpreting and discussing the review's findings (acknowledged as a scoping limitation in Section 5.5).

While the authors note contextual variation in camp water/latrine ratios and differing timeline definitions of the transitional phase, results across heterogeneous primary designs, secondary reviews, and guidelines are tallied together without systematic investigation of how methodological or contextual heterogeneity explains variation in empirical findings.
In the provided 39-page accepted manuscript, neither sources of funding for conducting the review nor authors' competing interests/conflicts of interest are reported.

raw_response.methodological_notes: 1. Review design & AMSTAR 2 fit: Cooper et al. (2021) is a PRISMA/JBI-guided 'systematic scoping review' (companion to Behnke et al., 2020 on protracted displacement and Shackelford et al., 2020 on emergency displacement). It conducts broad multi-database and grey-literature searches and duplicate Covidence screening, with a PRISMA flow diagram (Figure 1), but performs no risk-of-bias/quality appraisal of the 84 peer-reviewed studies (only AACODS credibility screening on 4 grey literature records) and synthesizes findings via unstratified study counts. Hence AMSTAR 2 fit is 'borderline_scoping_realist_or_hybrid' and overall AMSTAR 2 confidence is 'Critically Low' (critical flaws on Q2, Q7, Q9, Q13). 2. Narrow Criterion 2 audit: Fails narrow Criterion 2 (E03). The review broadly maps environmental health conditions, pathogen exposures (e.g., Vibrio cholerae, malaria, measles), and clinical outcomes in refugee/IDP camps 6 months to 2 years post-displacement. Although Table 12 includes a sub-bullet for 'Legal/policy environments' under institutional obstacles, the text cites only one healthcare-seeking survey regarding camp-confinement policies (Mohamed et al., 2014) alongside general NGO/municipal coordination and project-duration issues (UNICEF and Hydroconseil, 2017; Tota-Maharaj, 2016; Schuller and Levey, 2014), rather than empirically analyzing legal, regulatory, tenure, tariff, or ownership rules governing WASH access. 3. Primary-study list & double-counting alert: The review reports 88 included transitional-phase publications, whose full study-by-study extraction matrices reside in external online supplements S3 and S4 (not printed in the 39-page PDF). Forty-nine of the 88 included records (including all 4 grey literature items) are explicitly named inline across Section 3 Results and Tables 9-10 and are extracted here (excluding benchmark standards cited inside Table 9/10 right-hand columns and Discussion-only background citations such as Ziersch et al. 2017, Hashmi et al. 2019, and Abbas et al. 2018). Crucially, Table 5 reveals that 18 of the 88 'included studies' (20%) are themselves secondary literature/systematic reviews (e.g., Ramesh et al. 2015, De Buck et al. 2015, Kimbrough et al. 2012, Rebaudet et al. 2013, Cronin et al. 2008) and 2 are guidelines, creating substantial secondary-on-secondary overlap risk if treated as primary studies.
